1. Normal Pancreas and Congenital Abnormalities

How to use thisDr. McCuen's series covers the exocrine pancreas only (endocrine pancreas is another block). In her slide tables, red = highest-yield items. Her study-guide key answers appear as collapsed reveals.

Normal review

  • Lobular organ beneath the stomach next to the duodenum: head (attached to duodenum), neck, body, tail. Secretes through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum.
  • Acinar cells (~85%): exocrine; make zymogens (proenzymes). Islets of Langerhans: endocrine.
  • The main duct normally drains via the major papilla (papilla of Vater, duct of Wirsung); the accessory duct drains via the minor papilla (duct of Santorini).

Developmental anomalies

AnomalyDefectClinical
Pancreas divisumFailure of fusion of ventral and dorsal pancreatic ducts; the duct of Santorini drains most of the gland through the small minor papilla, limiting drainageMost common congenital anomaly; usually asymptomatic/incidental; ~5% develop pancreatitis (often with another predisposing factor)
Annular pancreasPancreatic tissue encircling the duodenum from incomplete rotationOften asymptomatic; can narrow and obstruct the duodenum (outflow obstruction)
Heterotopic (ectopic) pancreasPancreatic tissue at abnormal sites ("pancreatic rests"); most common in the stomach, then along the small intestineUsually asymptomatic; larger rests cause obstruction or pain; can still develop cysts or neoplasms like normal pancreas
Pancreas divisum (slide 7) (click to enlarge)
Annular pancreas (slide 8) (click to enlarge)
Heterotopic pancreas (slide 9) (click to enlarge)

Cystic fibrosis in the pancreas

  • Autosomal recessive; defective CFTR (regulates chloride and bicarbonate transport) → ↓ Cl-/HCO3- secretion, ↑ sodium and water absorption → dehydrated, viscous, acidic secretions.
  • Mucus obstructs ducts → ↑ intraluminal pressure, ductal dilation, rupture and leakage of enzymes, inflammation, acinar cell damage and fibrosis.
  • Complications: pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea, vitamin deficiency) and chronic inflammation → fibrosis → chronic pancreatitis.
CFTR defect and pancreatic duct obstruction (slide 12) (click to enlarge)
CF pancreas: ductal dilation, inflammation, fibrosis (slide 14) (click to enlarge)
Describe the CF mechanism in the pancreas and how it resembles the lungs.Mutant CFTR impairs chloride and bicarbonate and increases sodium and water absorption, giving viscous secretions. In the pancreas these obstruct ducts → ↑ intraluminal pressure, acinar injury and inflammation. In the lungs the same viscous mucus obstructs airways, again causing pressure, cell damage and inflammation.
List and describe 3 developmental abnormalities of the pancreas.Divisum (failure of ventral/dorsal duct fusion); annular (tissue encircling the duodenum); heterotopic (pancreatic tissue at abnormal sites).

2. Pancreatitis: Mechanisms and Acute Pancreatitis

Protective mechanisms against autodigestion (pancreatitis = their failure)

  • Acinar cells secrete zymogens (inactive proenzymes). Trypsinogen is normally activated to trypsin only in the small bowel by enterokinase; trypsin then activates other enzymes.
  • Acinar and ductal cells secrete trypsin inhibitors (SPINK1) to prevent premature activation.
  • Intraductal pressure stays low, allowing free flow out of the gland.

Acute pancreatitis

Often reversible inflammation and destruction of pancreatic tissue from premature enzyme activation and autodigestion. Two mechanisms: duct obstruction and primary acinar cell injury. Two most common causes: gallstones and alcohol. Others: drugs, hyperlipidemia, ischemia, genetics.

Pathogenesis: duct obstruction (gallstone)

  1. Stone blocks drainage → ↑ intraluminal pressure.
  2. ↓ zymogen secretion; zymogens and fluid accumulate in acinar cells.
  3. Impaired calcium signaling (calcium builds up inside the cell), mitochondrial dysfunction (↓ ATP) and altered vesicle trafficking.
  4. Lysosomes fuse with zymogen granules; cathepsin B activates trypsinogen → trypsin → autodigestion, acinar cell death.
  5. Inflammatory response (cell death, fluid leak into the interstitium) → edema → compressed vessels → impaired blood flow → local ischemia, which perpetuates damage.

Alcohol: same pathway, different start: alcohol metabolism → reactive oxygen species (direct acinar injury) and fatty acid ethyl esters that impair calcium signaling.

Ways trypsinogen is prematurely activated

  • Normal: enterokinase (in the duodenum). Aberrant: cathepsin B (after calcium-driven lysosome fusion) and autoactivation (trypsin activating trypsinogen, positive feedback).
Trypsinogen activation and trypsin targets (slide 29) (click to enlarge)
Enzyme activated by trypsinDamage
ElastaseDegrades elastin and connective tissue (vessel destruction)
Proteases (chymotrypsin)Break down cellular proteins
AmylaseBreaks down starch/glycogen
LipaseBreaks triglycerides into fatty acids: fat necrosis
Phospholipase (FYI)Breaks down cell membranes

Hereditary causes (recurrent acute → chronic pancreatitis, often in childhood)

GeneMutationEffect
PRSS1 (trypsinogen)Gain of functionTrypsinogen autoactivates more readily
SPINK1 (trypsin inhibitor)Loss of function (both copies)Regulatory inhibition fails
CFTRLoss of functionViscous secretions: duct obstruction
Describe at least 2 ways premature trypsinogen activation occurs.(1) Calcium buildup impairs trafficking, so zymogen granules fuse with lysosomes and cathepsin B activates trypsinogen. (2) Inherited mutations: PRSS1 autoactivation or SPINK1 impaired inhibition. Also trypsinogen can autoactivate. (If asked for causes: ductal obstruction and acinar injury.)
Identify 3 enzymes activated by trypsin and how each contributes.Elastase (breaks connective tissue/vessels), chymotrypsin (cellular proteins), lipase (fat necrosis); phospholipase (membranes, FYI).
Gallstones vs alcohol: mechanism of injury?Gallstones: ductal obstruction → ↑ luminal pressure and zymogen accumulation. Alcohol: direct acinar injury plus fatty acid ethyl esters that raise intracellular calcium by impairing signaling.

Morphology

  • Acute interstitial pancreatitis (earlier): edema, immune infiltrates, minimal necrosis.
  • Acute hemorrhagic/necrotizing pancreatitis (advanced): large-scale parenchymal necrosis, hemorrhage, and fat necrosis (peripancreatic fat too).
  • Fat necrosis: lipase leaks from injured acinar cells, breaks down fat, and fatty acids react with calcium to form calcium soaps (saponification): grossly yellow chalky nodules.
Acute interstitial pancreatitis: edema and infiltrates (slide 31) (click to enlarge)
Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis: hemorrhage, necrosis, fat necrosis (slide 32) (click to enlarge)
Morphologic features distinguishing interstitial vs necrotizing?Interstitial: edema, extensive immune infiltrates, minimal necrosis. Necrotizing: hemorrhage, fat necrosis, extensive acinar necrosis.
Calcium in pancreatitis vs hypocalcemia in patients?Excess intracellular calcium impairs trafficking and triggers premature trypsinogen activation. Later, fat necrosis saponification uses up calcium at the site of necrosis, so serum calcium falls. (Her narration says 'hypercalcemia may occur' but means hypocalcemia, per the slide.)

Clinical

  • Radiating epigastric pain (to the back), anorexia, nausea.
  • Dx: elevated serum amylase and lipase (lipase more sensitive and specific, stays up longer), hypocalcemia, ultrasound/CT.
  • Complications: pancreatic pseudocysts (fluid collects peripancreatically in a fibrous wall; can be huge), infection of necrosis, systemic organ failure (DIC, ARDS), chronic pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis alone does not raise cancer risk (but a tumor can cause it by duct obstruction).
Pancreatic pseudocyst on CT (slide 33) (click to enlarge)

3. Chronic Pancreatitis, Autoimmune Pancreatitis and Comparison

Irreversible inflammation and destruction of pancreatic tissue with fibrosis and parenchymal loss.

  • Causes: chronic alcohol (major cause in adults), duct obstruction, autoimmune disease, genetic mutations. Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause in children.
  • Mechanism: recurrent acute pancreatitis → cycles of injury/healing release TGF-β and PDGF → activate pancreatic stellate cells → collagen deposition and ECM remodeling and fibrosis; acinar loss; pancreatic insufficiency.

Morphology

  • Gross: dense white fibrosis, calcification/calculi in ducts.
  • Triad microscopically: ductal dilation (with protein plugs in alcohol-related disease), dense fibrosis, acinar cell atrophy/loss.
Chronic pancreatitis: calculi, dilated ducts, fibrosis, acinar loss (slide 36) (click to enlarge)

Autoimmune pancreatitis

TypeFeatures
Type 1IgG4 from plasma cells; T-cell-mediated, multi-organ disease; lymphoplasmacytic sclerosis; IgG4 immunostain positive
Type 2Not IgG4; pancreas only; granulocytic epithelial lesions (neutrophils)
Type 3Immune checkpoint inhibitor adverse event; inflammation typically subsides when stopped
Autoimmune pancreatitis types 1, 2 and 3 (slide 38) (click to enlarge)

Clinical

  • Persistent abdominal and back pain (not the radiating acute pattern). Amylase/lipase not elevated. CT: calcifications.
  • Complications: pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea, malabsorption), diabetes mellitus (islet involvement), pancreatic adenocarcinoma (especially alcohol-related).
3 histologic findings of chronic pancreatitis and why they cause complications?Acinar atrophy, ductal distortion/dilation, diffuse fibrosis. Acinar loss and fibrosis reduce enzyme release (exocrine insufficiency, steatorrhea); architectural distortion impairs islets (diabetes); chronic injury is mutagenic and can progress to PDAC.
Differentiate the 3 types of autoimmune pancreatitis.Type 1: IgG4, lymphoplasmacytic sclerosis, multi-organ. Type 2: granulocytic epithelial lesions, pancreas only. Type 3: checkpoint-inhibitor associated.

Acute vs chronic (her table)

AcuteChronic
DefinitionOften reversible inflammation/destructionIrreversible inflammation/destruction
CausesAlcohol, gallstones (duct obstruction), drugs, hyperlipidemia, ischemia, geneticsAlcohol, obstruction, genetics, autoimmune
Mechanism↑ intracellular calcium → premature enzyme activation → acinar damage and inflammationRecurrent acute pancreatitis → ECM remodeling and fibrosis
MorphologyGross: fat necrosis, hemorrhage. Micro: fat necrosis, hemorrhage, infiltrates, edemaGross: fibrosis, calcification. Micro: ductal dilation, protein plugs, fibrosis, acinar atrophy/loss
ComplicationsPseudocysts, hypocalcemia, infection, organ failure, chronic pancreatitisInsufficiency, diabetes, adenocarcinoma

4. Non-neoplastic Cysts

True cystPseudocyst
LiningThin epithelial layerFibrous/inflammatory (granulation) tissue, no epithelium
OriginCongenital; associated with polycystic kidney disease and von Hippel-Lindau diseasePancreatic fluid leaks and collects; from alcohol-associated acute pancreatitis or trauma
True cyst: epithelial lining (slide 44) (click to enlarge)
Pseudocyst: non-epithelial lining (slide 45) (click to enlarge)

Pseudocysts can be very large and obstructive.

True cyst vs pseudocyst?A true cyst has an epithelial lining; a pseudocyst does not and is surrounded by granulation tissue and fibrosis.

5. Cystic Neoplasms: SCN, MCN, IPMN, SPN

SCN (serous)MCN (mucinous)IPMNSPN
SiteTail, sometimes bodyTail, sometimes bodyHead (ducts)Anywhere
EpidemiologyOlder (elderly) femalesMiddle-aged females (95%)Slight male prevalence, olderYoung women (10:1)
PathogenesisVHL inactivation; benignKRAS, RNF43 (TP53, SMAD4 with transformation); precancerousKRAS, RNF43, GNAS (TP53, SMAD4 with transformation); precancerousCTNNB1 (β-catenin); low malignant potential
GrossCentral stellate scar, honeycomb microcystsLarge multilocular mucin-filled cystCyst attached to duct, papillary, mucin; may be multilocularSolid and cystic, hemorrhagic fluid
MicroMicrocysts lined by cuboidal epithelium, clear fluidMucin-secreting columnar epithelium over ovarian stromaPapillary architecture; intestinal, gastric or pancreaticobiliary epitheliumPseudopapillary sheets (poorly cohesive)
Serous cystic neoplasm (slide 47) (click to enlarge)
  • SCN: surgical resection is often curative; may be associated with VHL syndrome.
Mucinous cystic neoplasm (slide 48) (click to enlarge)
  • MCN: about half have KRAS, a third RNF43. Ovarian-type stroma (dense spindle cells, whorled) underlies the epithelium; thought to arise from primordial ovarian cells seeded in embryogenesis, explaining female predominance; grows in middle age with hormone/growth factor changes. Stroma stains for PR, ER and inhibin.
IPMN: duct involvement, papillary architecture, MUC stains (slide 49) (click to enlarge)
  • IPMN: ~80% KRAS, ~50% RNF43, ~60% GNAS. Epithelium varies: intestinal (MUC1 −, MUC2 +), gastric (both −), pancreaticobiliary (MUC1 +, MUC2 −); the type influences malignant behavior.
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (slide 50) (click to enlarge)
  • SPN: rare; CTNNB1 only key mutation; cells grow in sheets that break apart around vessels (pseudopapillae) and bleed (hemorrhagic cystic areas). IHC: nuclear/diffuse β-catenin and loss of E-cadherin (explains poor adhesion).
MCN almost always occurs in women: what supports this?Ovarian-type stroma expressing estrogen and progesterone receptors suggests hormone-responsive differentiation.
One characteristic gross feature of each neoplasm?SCN: central scar, honeycomb microcystic. MCN: large multilocular mucin-filled cyst. IPMN: large, potentially multilocular mucin-filled cyst connected to a duct. SPN: mixed solid and hemorrhagic cystic.

6. Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC)

  • Malignant tumor of the ductal epithelium; most common exocrine pancreatic tumor; poorest survival of common cancers (5-year survival ~5-13%).
  • Risk factors: age (>60), smoking (doubles risk), chronic pancreatitis (especially with alcohol), family history/genetic predisposition.
  • Other solid tumors mentioned only: acinar cell carcinoma, pancreatoblastoma (children); neuroendocrine tumors are covered elsewhere.

Pathogenesis: precursor lesions

PanIN (pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia): ~80%, plus MCN and IPMN.

PanIN progression with KRAS, CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 (slide 58) (click to enlarge)
StageMolecular eventContribution
Normal duct → low-grade PanIN (columnar, mucin-producing)KRAS activation (~90% of low grade), then CDKN2A (p16) loss↑ proliferation; loss of cell-cycle control
High-grade PanIN (carcinoma in situ): prominent papillary architecture, loss of polarity, cribriformTP53 and SMAD4 lossImpaired DNA damage response; escape from growth inhibition
Invasive PDACInvades surrounding tissue

Morphology

  • Location: head 60%, body 15%, tail 5% (narration says "most often head, rarely tail").
  • Gross: infiltrative mass invading neighboring tissue and ducts ("spiderweb"). Micro: abnormal glands in a desmoplastic stroma; perineural invasion characteristic.
PDAC: local invasion and desmoplastic stroma (slide 59) (click to enlarge)

Clinical presentation

  • Bile duct obstruction → jaundice (painless; usually later; head tumors present earlier).
  • Perineural invasion → abdominal or back pain.
  • Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign) (tumor products promote coagulation).
  • New-onset diabetes (islet damage); pancreatitis from duct obstruction.
  • Metastasis at diagnosis is common (lymph nodes, liver, lung).

Surgery

  • 85% unresectable. Tail tumor: distal pancreatectomy. Head tumor: Whipple (removes pancreatic head, duodenum, often gallbladder and part of stomach, then reconnects): extreme, many complications, one of the only potentially curative options.
Before and after Whipple procedure (slide 61) (click to enlarge)
3 complications of PDAC and how the tumor causes each?Jaundice (head tumor obstructs bile duct); pain (perineural invasion); Trousseau sign (tumor products activate coagulation); diabetes (islet damage); pancreatitis (duct obstruction).
How does location affect presentation and prognosis?Head: jaundice early, earlier detection, but resection (Whipple) is challenging. Body/tail: few symptoms, detected late, worse prognosis.
Molecular order driving PanIN?KRAS activation → CDKN2A inactivation → TP53 and SMAD4 inactivation.
